name: Chicago school of economics
summary: The Chicago school is the free-market, neoclassical price-theory tradition of University of Chicago economists, above all Milton Friedman and George Stigler. It holds that competitive markets allocate resources better than government, that money-supply control is the key to economic stability, and that government should be limited to enforcing rules, defending property and supplying a few public goods, with discretionary intervention and regulation avoided.
scope: The second Chicago school of Friedman and Stigler (1950s onward) as Hamowy and the New World Encyclopedia define it: price theory, monetarism and free-market policy advocacy. Answers come from Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom, which Hamowy ties to the school through Friedman. Not covered: the early Knight/Viner/Simons generation as such, the law-and-economics and new-classical strands, Austrian economists who taught at Chicago, and the later political uses of its ideas.

notes: Defined by Hamowy and the New World Encyclopedia; the New World entry is derived from Wikipedia and is used only for scope. Answers rest on Capitalism and Freedom (Friedman); nothing from Stigler or Becker was cited because their Nobel lectures are descriptive of method and settle none of the bank statements. Friedman's later positions outside the book (drugs, sex work) and the Chicago Boys in Chile were left out: they are one economist's views or another movement's record, not stated tenets of the school in the defining sources. Themes searched in the saved texts: markets and regulation, money and central banking, trade and exchange rates, taxation and inheritance, welfare, pensions, education, discrimination and segregation, unions and monopoly, speech and political freedom, majority rule and constitutions, decentralization, property, distribution and Marxist claims, conscription, charity. Silent on: religion, sexuality, family, ecology, technology, war and alliances, immigration, nationalism, gender.
